name: Lexical Collocation Strength
description: Analyzes the statistical probability of word pairings (Pointwise Mutual Information) to expose safe, mathematically highly probable phrase combinations.
mechanism: Rooted in the foundational computational linguistics work of Church & Hanks, this method calculates the Pointwise Mutual Information (PMI) of adjacent and nearby word pairs against massive baseline corpora. Large Language Models generate text by autoregressively predicting the most statistically probable next tokens. This mathematical nature inherently saddles them with a heavy, inescapable reliance on strong, common collocations (e.g., clichés, idiomatic chunks, expected adjective-noun pairs like 'tapestry of' or 'vibrant landscape'). In contrast, authentic human writers frequently invent novel, low-probability collocations, jarring associations, or creative metaphors that break statistical norms. By aggregating the overall PMI score of a text's n-grams, this method effectively identifies the mathematically 'safest' and most probable text configurations indicative of machine generation.
useCase: Identifying AI writing through its complete lack of novel, creative, or mathematically unexpected word pairings, exposing texts that are fundamentally built on clichés and 'safe' word associations.
strengths:
• Deeply exploits the core mechanical nature of autoregressive next-token prediction algorithms.
• Incredibly robust and effective regardless of the overarching topic, domain, or subject matter.
• Computationally lightweight assuming pre-compiled PMI baseline tables are loaded.
limitations:
• Dense academic writing or highly formalized legal drafting also heavily relies on strict, established, high-probability collocations, which can trigger severe false positives.
• Requires generating and continuously maintaining massive, up-to-date baseline frequency corpora for every single supported language.
• Creative prompt engineering (e.g., 'write in a surrealist style') can artificially lower PMI and occasionally bypass the filter.
parameters:
Analysis: Bigram/Trigram PMI Mapping
Metric: Average Collocation Probability vs. Lexical Novelty
Output: 0-100 Collocation Predictability Score
accuracy: High — 78-86%. One of the most robust, deeply foundational statistical markers of AI-generated text.

references.title: Church, K. W. & Hanks, P. (1990). Word Association Norms, Mutual Information, and Lexicography. Computational Linguistics.
Evert, S. (2008). Corpora and Collocations. Corpus Linguistics: An International Handbook.
Clark, E. et al. (2021). All That's 'Human' Is Not Gold: Evaluating Human Evaluation of Generated Text. ACL.
